title: Quick Take — Veridical Data Science (audiobook)
description: This book is about practicing data science in a way that is genuinely trustworthy. The central argument is that getting useful, reliable results from data requires more than applying algorithms — it requires critical thinking, domain knowledge, and a principled framework for evaluating whether your results hold up. The authors call this veridical, meaning truthful, data science.

title: Ch. 1 — An Introduction to Veridical Data Science
description: To practice veridical data science is to practice "truthful" data science. The goal is to answer real-world questions by collecting and critically evaluating relevant empirical, data-driven evidence, using human judgment calls in the context of domain knowledge. If that evidence is deemed sufficiently trustworthy, it gets communicated to domain stakeholders, where it can play a role in real-world decision making and in updating what we know about the domain.

title: Ch. 2 — The Data Science Life Cycle
description: Every data science project progresses through some combination of six stages. The book calls these stages together the data science life cycle, or DSLC. The six stages, in order, are: first, domain problem formulation and data collection; second, data cleaning, preprocessing, and exploratory data analysis; third, exploration of intrinsic data structures through dimensionality reduction and clustering; fourth, predictive and inferential analysis; fifth, evaluation of results; and sixth, communication of results. Almost every project will pass through stages one, two, five, and six. Stages three and four are optional — whether you need them depends entirely on the question you are asking.

title: Ch. 3 — Setting Up Your Data Science Project
description: In this chapter, we step back from the analytical substance of data science and look at the scaffolding around it — how you structure your files, write and document your code, and organize your workflow so that your results are reproducible and your project remains intelligible to collaborators and to your future self. The ideas here draw directly on the data science life cycle and the predictability, computability, and stability framework introduced earlier in the book.

title: Ch. 4 — Data Preparation
description: Every data science project begins with a question and a dataset, but rarely does the dataset arrive ready to use. The chapter opens with a concrete image: you are a journalist, or perhaps a researcher, trying to understand organ donation rates around the world. Before you can answer any question about trends or rankings, you need to confront the data itself — its inconsistencies, its missing entries, its inconvenient formatting. That confrontation is the subject of this chapter.

title: Ch. 5 — Exploratory Data Analysis
description: Since our eyes and brains are not wired to detect patterns in large tables filled with text and numbers, we almost never communicate data-driven results by simply handing someone the raw data. Instead, we summarize it — using a mean, a table, a chart — so that shape, distance, color, and size can do the work of conveying magnitude and relationship.

title: Ch. 6 — Principal Component Analysis
description: Answering sophisticated domain questions often involves data that is high-dimensional — data containing a large number of variables. A vivid example is biological gene expression data, which quantifies how actively each gene in the genome is being expressed. Since every person has more than 20,000 genes, every person's gene expression profile is itself a vector of more than 20,000 numbers. The question of how to explore relationships and interactions across 20,000 variables at once is not a simple one. Most of the visualization techniques we rely on — histograms, scatterplots — are designed for examining a few variables at a time and break down entirely at this scale. And it is not only visualization that struggles. Many analytic methods, including predictive models, perform poorly or fail outright when there are more variables than observations.
